y-m-10-05.title: Finding decimal pairs wey add up to 1
y-m-10-05.topic: Sum of one-decimal-place number and two-decimal-place number (sums by place under decimal point)
y-m-10-05.goal: Decide whether adding one-decimal-place number and two-decimal-place number fit make 1, make pairs of two-decimal-place numbers wey sum to 1, and describe pattern in digit sums for each place.
y-m-10-05.material: For dis activity, 'one-decimal-place number' mean number with one digit after decimal point, like 0.4; 'two-decimal-place number' mean number wey second digit after decimal no be 0, like 0.35. 0.30 equal 0.3, so e count as one-decimal-place number. All numbers bigger than 0.
y-m-10-05.thinking.0: First decide possible or impossible, then find evidence
y-m-10-05.thinking.1: Distinguishing few tests from explanation based on place value
y-m-10-05.prereq.0: Place values of one-decimal-place and two-decimal-place numbers (Grade 4 level)
y-m-10-05.prereq.1: Experience adding decimals by lining up decimal points
y-m-10-05.s.s1.prompt: If you add one one-decimal-place number and one two-decimal-place number, any pair fit make exactly 1?
y-m-10-05.s.s1.hint.0: Rewrite in your own words how di given rule separate 'decimal with one decimal place' from 'decimal with two decimal places', and check choices against rule.
y-m-10-05.s.s1.hint.1: Choose one one-decimal-place number and one two-decimal-place number, add dem, then write only second digit after decimal point in sum.
y-m-10-05.s.s1.o.a: No. Hundredths digit in sum na the same as hundredths digit of two-decimal-place number, so e no fit be 0
y-m-10-05.s.s1.r.a: Dis try explain by looking separately at digit for each place after decimal point.
y-m-10-05.s.s1.o.b: Yes. Find pair like 0.4 and 0.6 wey sum to 1
y-m-10-05.s.s1.r.b: Read di rule again and check whether 0.6 get one decimal place or 2 decimal places.
y-m-10-05.s.s1.o.c: E get. You fit find pair wey sum to 1, like 0.55 and 0.45.
y-m-10-05.s.s1.r.c: You find pair wey sum to 1, but check whether both numbers be di same kind.
y-m-10-05.s.s1.o.d: If I add plenty pairs and e no happen, I fit say e no dey, but I never try every pair, so I no sure.
y-m-10-05.s.s1.r.d: You make judgment from result of some tests, but you also think about how sure you fit be.
y-m-10-05.s.s1.explain: A number with one decimal place get empty second decimal place (na 0). So di second decimal digit of di sum na just di second digit of di number with 2 decimal places, and according to di agreement dat digit no be 0. For di sum to be 1 (= 1.00), di second place suppose be 0, so no such pair dey. Testing plenty pairs na good start, and explaining with place value cover every case at once.
y-m-10-05.s.s1.acc.0: You point out correctly say tests alone no fit guarantee “all cases.” If you fit explain with place value, you fit say e certain.
y-m-10-05.s.s2.prompt: Dis time, find pairs of 2 numbers with 2 decimal places wey add up to exactly 1. Both numbers must get second digit after decimal point wey no be 0. Make 3 different pairs. (Pair wey only change order count as same pair.)
y-m-10-05.s.s2.hint.0: Choose one number first, then check say di value you get by subtracting am from 1 no get 0 for second place.
y-m-10-05.s.s2.hint.1: Write each pair wey you make by separating first and second decimal places, then compare di sum of digits for each place.
y-m-10-05.s.s2.ok.c2: Both numbers reach di second decimal place.
y-m-10-05.s.s2.fail.c2: There are more than 2 digits after decimal point (third place or more), or di digits no fit.
y-m-10-05.s.s2.ok.c3: For both numbers, di second decimal digit no be 0.
y-m-10-05.s.s2.fail.c3: One number get 0 as second decimal digit (example: 0.4). 0.4 na number with one decimal place.
y-m-10-05.s.s2.explain: Pairs like 0.35+0.65, 0.12+0.88, and 0.99+0.01 dey. Di numbers with one decimal place, 0.4 and 0.6, no follow dis agreement. If one number second decimal digit na 5, di other number second digit must also be 5 (5+5=10).
y-m-10-05.s.s3.prompt: For pairs wey sum to 1, wetin you get when you add first-decimal-place digits together and second-decimal-place digits together? Use one pair you make as example and write di pattern.
y-m-10-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write one pair you make lined up vertically, then add di first-decimal-place digits and second-decimal-place digits separately.
y-m-10-05.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether other pairs give di same values.
y-m-10-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You write clearly say di sum of first places and di sum of second places be different values?
y-m-10-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You check whether di pattern work for pairs apart from di one you choose?
y-m-10-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You explain wetin happen for di first place when di sum of second places na 10?
y-m-10-05.s.s3.model.0: Di first-decimal-place digits sum to 9, and di second-decimal-place digits sum to 10. For 0.35 and 0.65, na also 3+6=9 and 5+5=10.
y-m-10-05.s.s3.model.1: Di second places sum to 10, so carry 1 go di first place. Di first places sum to 9, so when dem collect di 1, dem make 10 and carry another 1 to give 1. I check with 0.12 and 0.88.
y-m-10-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: Dis answer explain di pattern with carrying.

y-m-10-01.title: Which village get more people?
y-m-10-01.topic: Comparing big numbers (number of digits, then compare from di highest place)
y-m-10-01.goal: Explain how to decide which number bigger when di numbers get different number of digits, and which place digit decide am when dem get di same number of digits. Decide wetin you need know to compare when one digit hide.
y-m-10-01.material: You wan compare how many people live for Garam Village (가람마을) and Narae Village (나래마을). All numbers for di sign na natural numbers, dem write comma (,) after every 3 digits, and di first digit no be 0. Di unit na “명” (people).
y-m-10-01.thinking.0: Decide whether information enough to compare
y-m-10-01.thinking.1: Use if-then sentence to explain why we compare from di highest place
y-m-10-01.thinking.2: Separate “di exact value” from “enough information to compare”
y-m-10-01.prereq.0: Place value and how to read big numbers up to millions (Grade 4 level)
y-m-10-01.prereq.1: Read numbers wey dem write comma after every 3 digits
y-m-10-01.s.s1.prompt: First, case wey you fit see all digits. Garam Village get 987,654 people (nine hundred eighty-seven thousand six hundred fifty-four), and Narae Village get 1,000,000 people (one million). Which village get more people?
y-m-10-01.s.s1.hint.0: Count digits to see how many digits each number get.
y-m-10-01.s.s1.hint.1: Think how much you need add to 987,654 to get 1,000,000, and check di difference between di 2 numbers.
y-m-10-01.s.s1.o.a: Garam Village. Big digits like 9, 8, 7 dey first, so e bigger.
y-m-10-01.s.s1.r.a: You check how big di first digits be. Check whether di same method work when di numbers get di same number of digits and when dem get different number.
y-m-10-01.s.s1.o.b: Narae Village. Garam Village get 6-digit number and Narae Village get 7-digit number.
y-m-10-01.s.s1.r.b: Dis idea count di number of digits first, instead of looking at each digit.
y-m-10-01.s.s1.o.c: No fit decide. Di groups wey comma separate no be same number, so you no fit compare dem.
y-m-10-01.s.s1.r.c: You think say you no fit compare numbers if di comma groups differ. Commas na only marks wey make numbers easier to read. Think wetin decide di size of a number.
y-m-10-01.s.s1.explain: For natural numbers wey first digit no be 0, di one wey get more digits bigger. 987,654 na 6-digit number, and 1,000,000 na 7-digit number. Even if di first digits 9, 8, 7 look big, e no change am. You fit also check because adding 12,346 to 987,654 give 1,000,000.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.prompt: Dis time something stain di sign. Garam Village get 3,□45,678 people (□ na one hidden digit for hundred-thousands place), and Narae Village get 3,500,000 people (three million five hundred thousand). Wetin you need know to decide which village get more?
y-m-10-01.s.s2.hint.0: Write di 2 numbers side by side, starting from di highest place one place at a time, and find di first place wey di digits differ.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.hint.1: Try put 0 and 9 for □ and check whether di village wey get more change.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.o.a: Garam Village number get 45,678 for di back, and Narae Village back part na 00,000, so Garam Village bigger even if we no know □.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.r.a: You compare di numbers by di back parts. If di front digits differ for di same place, di back parts no affect di result. Put 0 for □ and compare directly.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.o.b: You fit decide only if you know exactly wetin □ be.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.r.b: You think say you must know exact value of □. Try put some digits for □ to check whether knowing only a range enough to compare.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.o.c: Knowing only whether □ na 4 or less, or 5 or more, enough to decide.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.r.c: You find di boundary where di comparison result change, and describe wetin you need as a “range,” not one “value.”
y-m-10-01.s.s2.o.d: Even if you no know □, compare di ones place: Garam Village 8 bigger than Narae Village 0, so Garam Village get more.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.r.d: You compare starting from di lowest place. Think which place you suppose check first when you compare big numbers.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.explain: Both numbers get 3 for millions place, so compare di next place, hundred-thousands. Narae Village get 5. If □ na 6~9, Garam Village bigger; if □ na 0~4, Narae Village bigger. If □ na 5, di hundred-thousands places equal, so check di next place. Ten-thousands place na 4 for Garam Village and 0 for Narae Village, so Garam Village bigger (3,545,678 > 3,500,000). So even if you no know exactly wetin □ be, e enough to know “na 4 or less, or 5 or more?”
y-m-10-01.s.s3.prompt: Di result change depending on di digit for □. Use conditions like “if □ na ...” to write which cases Garam Village get more and which cases Narae Village get more. Also write which place you compare to decide.
y-m-10-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write di number wey get 5 for □ and Narae Village number side by side, starting from di highest place.
y-m-10-01.s.s3.hint.1: First write which village get more when □ na 4 and when □ na 6.
y-m-10-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You check separately wetin happen when □ na 5?
y-m-10-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Your answer show di order: millions place equal, so you compare di next place?
y-m-10-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You check your cases by putting real digits (for example, 2 and 7) inside □?
y-m-10-01.s.s3.model.0: If □ na 5 or more, Garam Village get more; if □ na 4 or less, Narae Village get more. Both get 3 for millions place, so I compare □ for hundred-thousands place with 5.
y-m-10-01.s.s3.model.1: If □ na 4 or less, Narae Village get more; if □ dey from 5 to 9, Garam Village get more. Di highest place, millions, na di same, so I check di next place.
y-m-10-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: E no explain why e include □=5 inside 5 to 9, but e split di boundary correctly.

y-m-10-02.title: Seoa answer: we fit trust am?
y-m-10-02.topic: Checking result of (3-digit number)×(2-digit number) (estimation, ones digit, place alignment)
y-m-10-02.goal: Without doing di calculation again, use estimation and ones digit to find say di answer wrong, find di wrong line and explain why, and make your own multiplication wey pass both quick checks.
y-m-10-02.material: One notebook cost 347원. To find di price for 23 notebooks, Seoa do vertical multiplication and write answer as 1,735원. You fit see Seoa calculation for di second step. First, without doing di calculation again, think whether we fit trust dis answer.
y-m-10-02.thinking.0: Judge with reasons whether result make sense
y-m-10-02.thinking.2: Find di first line wey error happen
y-m-10-02.thinking.3: Make your own example wey meet di conditions
y-m-10-02.prereq.0: Experience calculating (3-digit number)×(1-digit number) and (2-digit number)×(2-digit number)
y-m-10-02.prereq.1: Experience estimating with nearby hundreds and tens numbers
y-m-10-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose all evidence wey you fit use to show say Seoa answer 1,735원 wrong. (Things wey you fit know without starting di calculation again.)
y-m-10-02.s.s1.hint.0: Think whether you fit estimate easily a value close to Seoa answer.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.hint.1: Try change 347 and 23 to nearby hundreds and tens numbers, or check which digits multiplication decide di ones digit of di product.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.o.a: 1,735 get 4 digits and 347×23 also seem to get 4 digits, so e look correct.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.r.a: You only check say di number of digits same. Four-digit numbers range widely from 1,000 to 9,999, so dis no enough to judge di size.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.o.b: If you take 347 as about 300 and 23 as about 20, di answer suppose be around 300×20=6,000, so 1,735 too small.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.r.b: You first estimate di rough size by changing di 2 numbers wey you multiply to nearby hundreds and tens numbers.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.o.c: If you calculate again di same way and get di same value, e correct.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.r.c: If you repeat di same method, you fit repeat di same mistake. Think of checking with another method.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.o.d: Since 7×3=21, ones digit of di product suppose be 1, but 1,735 end with 5.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.r.d: You use di rule say ones digit of product come from multiplying di ones digits.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.explain: b and d get same conclusion (answer no be 1,735) with different methods. b check di size, and d check di ones digit. a only say di number of digits same, so di evidence weak; c fit repeat di same mistake. Estimation or ones-digit check let you know say e “wrong,” but even if e pass both, you no fit conclude say e “correct.”
y-m-10-02.s.s1.acc.0: Estimation alone show say 1,735 too small. Ones-digit check (d) na separate evidence too.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.acc.1: Ones digit alone show say e wrong. Estimation wey check di size (b) na another evidence.
y-m-10-02.s.s2.prompt: Read Seoa solution line by line. Which line be di first wrong one?
y-m-10-02.s.s2.hint.0: Check one by one whether multiplication and addition for each line correct.
y-m-10-02.s.s2.hint.1: For each line, write wetin di number wey dem multiply really mean, then compare how dem line up di place values when dem add di products.
y-m-10-02.s.s2.line.0: First multiply with ones digit 3. 347 × 3 = 1041, so write 1041 for di first line.
y-m-10-02.s.s2.line.1: Multiply by tens digit 2. 347 × 2 = 694, so write 694 on second line, align am with right end of first line.
y-m-10-02.s.s2.explain: First mistake dey line 2. Di 2 for 23 na tens digit, so e mean 20, and you gatz add 347×20=6940. If you write 694 aligned at right end, you add 694, no be 6940. Addition for line 3 correct by itself, but both numbers wey dem add wrong, so conclusion for line 4 wrong too. Correct answer na 1041 + 6940 = 7981.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.prompt: Make two multiplications with different answers wey pass both estimate (product 6,000 or more and 8,000 or less) and ones-digit check (product end with 1). Multiplicand a na three-digit number and multiplier b na two-digit number. Dem don use 347×23 already, so no use am.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.hint.0: Ones digit of product na the same as ones digit of product of ones digits for both numbers. Find pairs of digits wey give value 1.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.hint.1: After choosing digit pair, change three-digit number and two-digit number and check with estimation whether product dey between 6,000 and 8,000.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.fail.c1: a must be natural number from 100 to 999.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.fail.c2: b must be natural number from 10 to 99.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.ok.c3: Product na 6,000 or more and 8,000 or less.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.fail.c3: Product no dey between 6,000 and 8,000. Try estimate am.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.fail.c4: Ones digit of product no be 1. Look at product of ones digits.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.fail.c5: Dem don use 347×23 already. Choose different a.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.explain: For example, 301×21=6321 and 249×29=7221 pass both checks. For ones digit to be 1, ones digits of both numbers must be (1, 1), (3, 7), (7, 3), or (9, 9). But answer wey calculate another place wrong fit pass same checks too. Checks useful to catch 'wrong' answers, but dem no guarantee 'right'.

y-m-10-03.s.s2.fail.c2: a must be natural number from 100 to 999.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.fail.c1: b must be natural number from 10 to 99.
y-m-10-03.title: Boxes for 200 apples
y-m-10-03.topic: Understanding quotient and remainder of division with remainder to fit situation
y-m-10-03.goal: Understand say same quotient and remainder fit be used as different answers when question change, and by making possible numbers for division with given quotient and remainder, check condition "remainder smaller than divisor".
y-m-10-03.material: Fruit shop get 200 apples. One box fit hold up to 12 apples. 200 divided by 12 give quotient 16 and remainder 8 (12×16=192 and 200-192=8).
y-m-10-03.thinking.0: Changing or keeping judgment based on new condition
y-m-10-03.thinking.1: Understanding same calculation result according to situation
y-m-10-03.thinking.2: Making several solutions wey fit conditions
y-m-10-03.prereq.0: Meaning of quotient and remainder in (three-digit number)÷(two-digit number)
y-m-10-03.prereq.1: Experience checking division with multiplication and addition
y-m-10-03.s.s1.prompt: Follow one information at a time to see how same calculation result (quotient 16, remainder 8) dey used depending on question.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.hint.0: Each time information come, explain in words where di 8 apples dey.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.hint.1: If each answer correct, check how many apples dey altogether by multiplying by 12.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.info: Owner talk, “I wan put apples inside boxes and keep dem.” Dem never talk anything else.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: How many boxes dem need? Choose your current thinking.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.after: If you understand "put dem in boxes and keep dem" as putting all inside, na 17 boxes; thinking say first check wetin to do with 8 apples reasonable too. 16 boxes na answer wey leave 8 apples nowhere.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You write only quotient as answer and no think wetin happen to remaining 8 apples.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: 17 boxes. Dem must put remaining 8 apples too, so one extra box need.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You understand am as putting remaining 8 apples inside another box too.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We no fit decide. We need know wetin to do with remaining 8 apples.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You find information wey question miss.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.info: Owner add, “I fit only sell customer boxes wey full with 12 apples.”
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: So how many boxes dem fit sell to customers?
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.after: 16 boxes full, and 8 apples remain because dem no fill one box. For dis question, quotient 16 na answer.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 17 boxes. Dem fit sell box with leftover apples too.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You no use new condition wey you just hear, 'only full boxes'.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 16 boxes. Dem only count full boxes, so na quotient.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You use condition say na only 'full boxes' dem count.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 8 boxes. Dem fit sell as many boxes as remainder.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You understand remainder 8 as number of boxes. Remainder mean number of apples wey remain.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.info: Owner change im mind. “Make we no throw away leftover apples; put dem all inside boxes and keep dem for warehouse. One box fit hold up to 12 apples.”
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: How many boxes dem go keep for warehouse, and how many apples go dey last box?
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.after: Out of 17 boxes, 16 hold 12 apples each, wey na 192, and last box get remaining 8 apples (192+8=200). To fill all 17 boxes, you need 12×17=204 apples, so 4 apples go short.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 16 boxes, and 12 apples in di last box
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You no decide where to put remaining 8 apples.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 17 boxes, and 12 apples for last box
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You count box number correctly, but check how many apples dey if all 17 boxes full.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 17 boxes, and 8 apples in last box
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You think of putting remainder inside last box.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.reflect: At first, both b and c reasonable (because we no know wetin to do with 8 apples). According to new condition, answer become 16 or 17. Even with same calculation, if question about 'full ones only' or 'all of dem', use quotient as e be or add 1 to quotient.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.prompt: Dis time, make we think backward. Three-digit number a divided by two-digit number b, quotient 15 and remainder 17 (division: a ÷ b = 15 … 17). Make two pairs of a and b like dis, with different b values.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.hint.0: Rewrite "quotient na 15 and remainder na 17" as "b fit enter some number of times and something remain", and write expression for a using b. Then choose one value for b and make a.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.hint.1: Really divide a wey you make by b to check quotient 15 and remainder 17, and compare remainder with b.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.fail.c3: a no be number wey you get by adding 17 to b×15. Try build a backward from quotient and remainder.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.fail.c4: Remainder 17 bigger than or equal to divisor b. If you really divide this equation, quotient and remainder go change.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.explain: a na b×15+17. For example, if b=20, then a=317, and 317÷20 give quotient 15 and remainder 17. But remainder must be smaller than divisor, so b must bigger than 17; and for a to be three-digit number, b must be 65 or less. So any natural b from 18 to 65 fit.
y-m-10-03.s.s3.prompt: Minho choose b=12 and a=197 and write "197 ÷ 12 = 15 … 17". Write why dis equation no fit be correct division result, and write actual quotient and remainder when 197 divided by 12.
y-m-10-03.s.s3.hint.0: Compare number wey remain after taking 12 away from 197 fifteen times with 12.
y-m-10-03.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether you fit take 12 away one more time from remainder, then write how quotient and remainder change.
y-m-10-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You look how many more times 12 fit enter remainder 17?
y-m-10-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You check actual quotient and remainder with 12×(quotient)+(remainder)=197?
y-m-10-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You explain with your own words why remainder must be smaller than divisor?
y-m-10-03.s.s3.model.0: Na because remainder 17 bigger than divisor 12. 12 fit enter 17 one more time, so if you really do 197÷12, quotient na 16 and remainder na 5.
y-m-10-03.s.s3.model.1: Number wey remain after dividing by 12 must smaller than 12, but 17 remain, so you fit divide one more time. So 197 = 12×16 + 5.
y-m-10-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: E use "number wey remain" instead of word "remainder", but e mean the same thing.
y-m-10-03.s.s3.model.2: 17 bigger than 12, so dem fit subtract 12 one more time, wey mean e wrong. 197÷12 get quotient 16 and remainder 5.

y-m-10-04.title: Fractions with denominator 7 wey whole-number part na 2
y-m-10-04.topic: Relationship between improper fractions and mixed numbers with same denominator (finding improper fractions with same whole-number part)
y-m-10-04.goal: Use estimation (comparing size) find wrong line in fraction solution, find all numerators wey fit condition, and generalize pattern. Explain why boundary cases wey turn whole numbers no count as mixed numbers.
y-m-10-04.material: Proper fraction na fraction wey numerator smaller than denominator; improper fraction na numerator equal or bigger than denominator; mixed number na whole number and proper fraction together (example: 2 and 3/7). Fraction wey equal whole number exactly, like 14/7, na whole number, no be mixed number. For dis activity, numerator na natural number.
y-m-10-04.thinking.1: Making several examples wey fit conditions
y-m-10-04.thinking.3: Reasoning about counting rule when denominator change
y-m-10-04.prereq.0: Names and meanings of proper fractions, improper fractions, and mixed numbers (Grade 4 level)
y-m-10-04.prereq.1: Experience changing whole number to fraction with same denominator
y-m-10-04.s.s1.prompt: Hangyeol write solution to change '3 and 2/5' to improper fraction. Which line first wrong?
y-m-10-04.s.s1.hint.0: First think which bigger, 3 and 2/5 or 3, then compare with final result of solution.
y-m-10-04.s.s1.hint.1: First check which fraction with denominator 5 represent whole number 1.
y-m-10-04.s.s1.line.0: Make we write whole number 3 in 3 and 2/5 as fraction with denominator 5.
y-m-10-04.s.s1.explain: First mistake na line 2. 1 na 5/5, so 3 na 15/5. 3/5 smaller than 1, so e no fit equal 3. Result for line 4 wrong too, because 3 and 2/5 bigger than 3 but e say 1. Correct solution add 15/5 and 2/5 to get 17/5.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.prompt: Among improper fractions with denominator 7, find three fractions wey whole-number part be 2 when you write dem as mixed number, and enter their numerators. (For □/7, □ na numerator. Since na mixed number, proper-fraction part must dey.)
y-m-10-04.s.s2.hint.0: When numerator na 7, 8, 9, … change □/7 to mixed number and write in table how whole-number part dey change.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.hint.1: From table, choose only rows where whole-number part na 2, compare numerators, and check whether proper-fraction part remain.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Numerator must be natural number 1 or more.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.ok.c2: Numerator bigger than or equal to denominator, so na improper fraction.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.fail.c2: If numerator smaller than 7, na proper fraction. Make am improper fraction.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.ok.c3: When you change am to mixed number, whole-number part na 2.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.fail.c3: When changed to mixed number, whole-number part no be 2. Check what □/7 equal 2.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.ok.c4: Proper-fraction part dey, so na mixed number.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.fail.c4: E be number wey exactly equal whole number. Choose numerator wey leave proper-fraction part.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.explain: 14/7 na whole number 2, and 21/7 na 3. Mixed numbers with whole-number part 2 na 2 and 1/7 through 2 and 6/7; when change dem to improper fractions, six dey, with numerators 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20.
y-m-10-04.s.s3.prompt: Dis time denominator na 9. When you write as mixed numbers, how many improper fractions get whole-number part 2?
y-m-10-04.s.s3.hint.0: When denominator na 9, write all numbers wey fit enter □ for mixed number 2 and □/9.
y-m-10-04.s.s3.hint.1: Check what number you get if □ na 0 or 9, and decide whether to include those two cases.
y-m-10-04.s.s3.o.a: 6. Count na the same even if denominator change
y-m-10-04.s.s3.r.a: You think count for denominator 7 stay the same. Check by listing numerators yourself for denominator 9.
y-m-10-04.s.s3.r.b: You include numerator 18. Check whether 18/9 na whole number or mixed number.
y-m-10-04.s.s3.r.c: You include both end numbers. Check what 18/9 and 27/9 equal.
y-m-10-04.s.s3.r.d: Dis na idea of counting without two ends, wey turn exactly to whole numbers.
y-m-10-04.s.s3.explain: Mixed numbers with whole-number part 2 na 2 and 1/9 through 2 and 8/9, wey be 8. When dem change to improper fractions, numerators na 19 to 26. 18/9 na 2 and 27/9 na 3, so dem no be mixed numbers. Count na 6 when denominator na 7 and 8 when na 9, so count equal (denominator - 1). Na because numerator of proper-fraction part fit be anything from 1 to (denominator - 1).

y-m-10-06.title: Can 3 months of records tell us wetin go happen next month?
y-m-10-06.topic: Counting forward by big numbers and di limit of predicting with a rule
y-m-10-06.goal: Predict di next number from records wey count by 100,000, but use counterexample show say few records no make am “certain,” and separate prediction from certainty.
y-m-10-06.material: Amusement park record how many visitors come each month. Di records only use units of 10,000 people, so dem always be multiples of 10,000. January get 3,420,000 people, February get 3,520,000 people, and March get 3,620,000 people. Mina talk, “E dey increase by 100,000 people each month, so April go definitely get 3,720,000 people!”
y-m-10-06.thinking.0: Judge how certain prediction based on rule be
y-m-10-06.thinking.2: Write prediction and sure claim as different things
y-m-10-06.prereq.0: Read and write big numbers using hundred-thousands and millions (Grade 4 level)
y-m-10-06.prereq.1: Count forward by a fixed number
y-m-10-06.s.s1.prompt: Which thinking best match wetin Mina talk?
y-m-10-06.s.s1.hint.0: Find how many people di number increase from January to February, and from February to March.
y-m-10-06.s.s1.hint.1: Think of one situation wey fit make April get different value (for example, weather or event), and consider whether di records alone fit tell you dat.
y-m-10-06.s.s1.o.a: Around 3,720,000 people na reasonable prediction, but different value fit happen.
y-m-10-06.s.s1.r.a: You read di rule from di records, and also separate prediction from certainty.
y-m-10-06.s.s1.o.b: 3,720,000 people definitely correct, because e increase by 100,000 for all 3 months.
y-m-10-06.s.s1.r.b: You conclude from di same thing happening 3 times say e go always happen. Think whether evidence show say e go happen same way di fourth time too.
y-m-10-06.s.s1.o.c: We no fit know April at all. Di first 3 records no use for prediction.
y-m-10-06.s.s1.r.c: You throw away all earlier records. Think whether dem fit give clue about di rule.
y-m-10-06.s.s1.o.d: E look like around 3,620,000 people, but e fit wrong.
y-m-10-06.s.s1.r.d: You talk carefully, but you no use di increase wey you fit read from di records.
y-m-10-06.s.s1.explain: Di fact say e increase by 100,000 for 3 months give clue say e likely go increase by similar amount for April too. But di increase fit different for April, so you no fit say “definitely.” Throwing away all di records (c) or ignoring di increase amount (d) no be good prediction either.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.prompt: Make records wey show Mina “definitely” fit be wrong. For January, February, and March, di number increase by 100,000 each time. For April, make am no be 100,000 more than March. All records na 7-digit numbers, and January and April na multiples of 10,000. Make 2 records with different increases for April.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.hint.0: Keep di first 3 months same as di example, then think of an April value wey no be 100,000 more than March.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.hint.1: After you choose April value, check say di difference from March no be 100,000 and e na multiple of 10,000.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Di records must be 7-digit numbers from 1,000,000 to 9,999,999.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.ok.c2: January and April na multiples of 10,000.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.fail.c2: January and April must be written in units of 10,000 people (multiples of 10,000).
y-m-10-06.s.s2.ok.c3: Di number increase by 100,000 people from January to February.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.fail.c3: February must be 100,000 more than January.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.ok.c4: Di number increase by 100,000 people from February to March.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.fail.c4: March must be 100,000 more than February.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.ok.c5: For April, e no increase by 100,000 people. Mina “definitely” don break.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.fail.c5: April na exactly 100,000 more than March. Then wetin Mina talk na exactly correct.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.explain: For example, 3,420,000 → 3,520,000 → 3,620,000 → 3,730,000 increase by 100,000 for first 3 months, then increase by 110,000 for April. Record wey go down, like 5,100,000 → 5,200,000 → 5,300,000 → 5,250,000, na also counterexample. If even one such record fit happen, records from only 3 months no fit make April “definitely” one thing.
y-m-10-06.s.s3.prompt: How you go predict number of people for April? Write your predicted number and reason. Also write wetin else you need know to help if your prediction fit wrong.
y-m-10-06.s.s3.hint.0: Put di records wey you make for s2 beside di first 3 records, then see how April fit different even though records stay same up to March.
y-m-10-06.s.s3.hint.1: Think of one case wey go make your prediction wrong, and write wetin you need know to find out.
y-m-10-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: I predict April go get around ... people. Because ...
y-m-10-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You explain how your predicted number come from di records?
y-m-10-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Your wording show say your prediction na “around,” not “definitely”?
y-m-10-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Wetin you wan know more about na something specific wey fit change your prediction?
y-m-10-06.s.s3.model.0: I predict April go get around 3,720,000 people. Na because e increase by 100,000 every month from January to March. But event or weather for April fit different, so I need know more about dat to be sure.
y-m-10-06.s.s3.model.1: I guess around 3,720,000 people, but I no fit say na definitely so. Na true say di same amount add for 3 months, but April fit change differently. If I also get May record, I fit trust di rule more.
y-m-10-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: E no turn di prediction into sure claim, and e talk exactly which extra records dem need.
